Hi Soojin,

Thanks again for the demo last week — the Dedicated option looks promising for our regulated workloads. Before our procurement team will move forward, they need clarity on a few technical commitments around data residency and deletion. Can you confirm the following for Dedicated deployments?

1) Can we pin our Dedicated cluster to a specific AWS region in the EU and prevent any cross-region replication of customer request payloads or cached KV state?

2) What is Redwood's standard retention window for request logs, audit trails, and cached prefixes/KV? Is that configurable per customer or per deployment?

3) Describe the deletion/erasure flow: how is data purged on customer request, what guarantees do you provide around propagation to backups and object storage, and how long until the entire footprint is removed?

4) Are encryption keys customer-managed (KMS/HSM) or Redwood-managed for Dedicated? If customer-managed, what is the KMS integration surface?

5) Can we get an SLA or contractual language we can share with our legal/procurement describing region isolation and deletion SLAs?

Procurement is on quick turnaround for the next quarter. If helpful, loop in engineering/security folks and we can set a 30-minute call.

Hi Emily — thanks for the clear list. Looping in Mateo (solutions) and Marcus (security) so we can provide written specifics and a short operational playbook. High-level answers below; we will follow up with a short doc and an SLA-ready paragraph for procurement.

Quick answers (high level):
- Yes: Dedicated clusters support region pinning. We can provision and pin to a single AWS region (e.g., eu-west-1) and configure routing to avoid cross-region fallbacks.
- Retention: Default retention for request logs/audit is 90 days; KV/prefix caches are configurable (default 7 days). We can propose custom retention windows in contracts.
- Deletion/erasure: We run a coordinated multi-step erasure workflow: invalidate runtime caches, delete persistent store records, purge object storage snapshots, and trigger background reclaim tasks. We aim for full removal within 30 days for standard retention items; backups and deep archives may require a longer, contract-defined window — details below.
- Keys: For Dedicated we support customer-managed KMS keys (AWS KMS) and can integrate with customer HSMs for on-prem. Redwood-managed keys are available if the customer prefers.

Next steps: I attached a short data-residency summary that outlines region pin options and the deletion workflow. Mateo will add implementation/configuration notes and Marcus will provide the security/compliance language. If procurement wants a 1-page addendum for the contract, we can draft that and share for review.

Available for a quick call Wed or Thu.

Marcus / Soojin — forwarding Emily's questions and my proposed configuration notes for Acme. Quick implementation notes for the EU-pinned Dedicated deployment: 

- Provisioning: spin up a Dedicated pool in eu-west-1, disable multi-AZ cross-region replication at the routing plane. API gateway and ingress stay in the same VPC/subnet range.
- KV cache: deploy with local SSD-backed cache nodes; configure automatic eviction after TTL (configurable). Ensure cache shards are not replicated to other regions.
- Persistent storage: application metadata and logs live in S3 buckets tagged and locked to eu-west-1; enable bucket-level policies to deny PutObject calls from other regions.
- Backups: snapshots are taken daily. For Acme, we should set lifecycle rules to keep snapshots in-region only and disable cross-region replication.
- Erasure: orchestration job sequence: 1) mark records for deletion, 2) scrub ephemeral SSDs, 3) delete S3 objects and snapshots, 4) remove database rows, 5) update audit log. We have a background job that removes soft-deletes based on retention TTL.

I can prepare a short technical appendix (1-2 pages) that we can attach to the procurement addendum. Also include example CLI/API calls to trigger an emergency erase for legal requests.

Emily (and team) — I wanted to add the security and compliance perspective and a proposed contractual commitment. Key points below. I attached a draft erasure SLA for procurement to review.

1) Region isolation and routing
- We will provision Dedicated compute and storage within the customer-selected AWS region. Network-level controls (VPC endpoints, security groups, route tables) prevent cross-region egress from runtime hosts.
- Fallback routing: by default we prefer single-region routing. We can add a strict region-lock policy to reject requests when local capacity is exceeded — this is the recommended approach for strict data residency.

2) Deletion guarantees and backups
- Erasure workflow: upon customer-initiated erase we will: invalidate caches (seconds), remove runtime artifacts (minutes-hours), delete objects from primary storage (within 24 hours), and enqueue snapshot cleanup. For standard configurations we commit to complete eradication from active systems within 30 days.
- Backups & archives: if you require guaranteed in-region-only retention and deletion, we must include that in contract language. Our standard backup retention may involve snapshot lifecycle policies; cross-region replication is opt-in and will be disabled by default for Dedicated.

3) Keys and encryption
- Customer-managed KMS: supported. We recommend customer-managed AWS KMS keys with key policies that limit Redwood's ability to export raw key materials. For higher assurance, HSM-backed keys via CloudHSM or on-prem HSM integration is supported in Private installations.

4) Auditability and evidence
- We can provide audit logs of deletion and retention actions, including timestamps and operator IDs. We can also provide periodic reports showing retention windows and recent erasure jobs.
- For procurement/legal: we can produce a one-page attestation describing region lock, deletion workflow, and expected timelines.

Attachments: I attached an erasure SLA draft (erasure-sla-draft.docx) + a short checklist for procurement. If Acme wants a stricter SLA (e.g., 14-day complete deletion), we can discuss a contract amendment with associated operational costs.

Happy to jump on a call to walk procurement through the language.

Regards,
